variants.name: tokio::sync::mpsc bounded channel (async)
variants.implementation_notes: The async realization is a bounded channel: tokio::sync::mpsc::channel(n) buffers n messages and send(msg).await does not complete while the buffer is full, so the backpressure propagates into the producer task without blocking the executor - the classic queue-plus-mutex-plus-condvar structure is replaced by the channel's internal synchronization plus a future. The bound is mandatory (capacity 0 panics, unlike std's rendezvous channel), and try_send's TrySendError::Full is the explicit shed path. For a slow consumer that is not the same task, an unbounded channel plus an await on the consumer's completion is not an alternative: choose the bound and let the producer wait.
pitfalls: Sending on a full bounded channel parks the task: if the consumer runs in the same task (or the producer awaits the consumer), the pipeline deadlocks.
Ignoring the Err from send() hides the case where the consumer died and work is silently dropped.
A blocking send or a std::sync channel inside an async runtime stalls the worker thread; move blocking producers into spawn_blocking.
try_send returning Full is load shedding, not backpressure - choosing it must be explicit and measured.

variants.name: std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel (threads)
variants.implementation_notes: For thread-based code the standard library already has the pattern: std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel(bound) returns a SyncSender whose send blocks when the internal buffer is full, and a bound of 0 makes it a rendezvous channel where every send waits for a matching recv - the classic queue is not hand-written. Use it when the stages are OS threads (or inside spawn_blocking), and prefer it over a Mutex<VecDeque> plus Condvar unless you need multi-consumer semantics or a priority policy. The bound is a real memory bound: n * size_of::<T>() plus bookkeeping is the worst case.
pitfalls: std::sync::mpsc supports a single consumer: a second Receiver clone is not possible, so fan-out needs a different structure.
sync_channel's blocking send is still a blocking call - calling it from async code parks a runtime worker thread.
Dropping the Receiver makes every later send return Err, and dropping the Sender ends the consumer's iterator; lifecycle must be deliberate.
A rendezvous bound (0) maximises pressure and can deadlock pipelines whose stages are not concurrently scheduled.

variants.name: futures::Sink poll_ready contract
variants.implementation_notes: Streaming APIs express the same handshake as a trait contract: futures::Sink::poll_ready must return Poll::Ready before each start_send, and Pending means 'full, wait for a wake-up' - that is the backpressure signal, and combinators such as send_all/forward propagate it through a whole stream-to-sink graph. Implementations buffer internally and usually flush to make room, so a bounded sink value (or one wrapping a bounded channel) is what keeps memory predictable. This is the classic pattern restated as a polling protocol: the bound lives inside the sink, the readiness poll is the blocking wait, and flush/close define the drain semantics.
pitfalls: Calling start_send without a successful poll_ready is a contract violation; implementations may silently reorder, drop or panic.
A Sink with an internal unbounded buffer (a Vec sink, some adapters) never applies pressure; wrap the real endpoint instead.
poll_ready's wake-up must be registered before returning Pending, otherwise the task is never rescheduled.
Mixing a bounded upstream channel with an unbounded sink buffer just moves the queue; the effective bound is the smallest one in the chain.
